# AN/PRC-117G Radio
The AN/PRC-117G is a manpack radio used by radio operators. It can carry up to four radio nets, relay combat communications over a larger area than a headset, operate as a field telephone, and store equipment.
If you only need to get the radio working, follow [bold]Quick start[/bold]. The remaining sections explain its other functions.
## Quick start
- [bold]Wear the radio[/bold] in your back slot. A carried or dropped radio does not provide relay coverage. - [bold]Open the radio panel.[/bold] Alt-click the radio, or right-click it and select [bold]Open Radio Panel[/bold]. Close the introductory briefing with [bold]GOT IT[/bold] if it appears. - On the [bold]NETS[/bold] tab, press [bold]LOAD STANDARD NETS[/bold]. This powers the radio, loads your standard nets, and selects your squad net for transmission. - [bold]Insert your COMSEC fill card.[/bold] Use the card on the radio. The SECURITY tab should display [bold]ENCRYPTED[/bold]. - Type [color=#a4885c]:r[/color] followed by your message to transmit on the memory marked [bold]ON AIR[/bold]. - Check the status banner below the display if the radio is not working. A green banner indicates normal operation.
The radio requires a power cell. Carrying a spare is recommended for extended operation.
## Controls
The AN/PRC-117G has two control interfaces:
- [textlink="Guided panel" link="AU14CommsANPRCGuided"] - provides the standard controls and keeps advanced settings in automatic mode. - [textlink="Expert faceplate" link="AU14CommsANPRCExpert"] - provides direct access to the radio's keypad, display, and advanced functions.
The guided panel is sufficient for normal operation.
## Operator training
Some AN/PRC functions require radio-operator training.
A trained operator can:
- open the radio control panel - transmit through the pack with [color=#a4885c]:r[/color] - provide relay coverage while wearing the radio - set the radio up as an unattended relay
The handset and field telephone do [bold]not[/bold] require radio-operator training.
### GOVFOR and OPFOR trained roles
- Commanding Officer, Adjutant, and staff officers - Engineering and intelligence officers - Synthetics - Squad Leaders and Fireteam Leaders - Radio Traffic Operators
### CLF trained roles
- Cell Leader - Radio Operator
Anyone can permanently learn to operate the radio by reading a [bold]field radio operator's pamphlet[/bold].
Ordinary headset users do not require radio training. They only need to be within relay range of a powered radio carrying their net.
## Relay coverage
Combat radio nets are [bold]relay-gated[/bold]. A headset can use a combat net only while within range of a relay carrying that net.
A powered AN/PRC worn by a trained operator relays [bold]every friendly combat net loaded into its memory[/bold]. The relayed net does not need to be the radio's current ON AIR memory.
If a squad net is loaded into the radio, nearby headsets assigned to that net can use it.
### Antennas
Relay range depends on the installed antenna.
[bold]Antenna[/bold] [bold]Clear[/bold] [bold]Degraded[/bold] [bold]Notes[/bold]
WHIP 30 tiles 45 tiles Standard antenna. Full range while moving.
WIRE 35 tiles 50 tiles Range is halved while moving.
MAST 55 tiles 80 tiles Range is halved while moving.
Relay coverage also extends one level above and below the radio.
### Output power
Output power modifies relay range:
- [bold]LO[/bold] - 60% - [bold]MED[/bold] - 100% - [bold]HI[/bold] - 150%
Output power is changed from the expert faceplate. The guided panel uses MED.
## Nets and memories
The AN/PRC has up to [bold]four memory slots[/bold].
A memory can contain:
- a named radio net - a direct frequency
[color=#a4885c]:r[/color] transmits through the memory marked [bold]ON AIR[/bold]. Press [bold]USE[/bold] beside another memory to select it.
[bold]LOAD STANDARD NETS[/bold] fills empty memories with the operator's standard squad and command nets. Manually configured memories are not overwritten.
[bold]EDIT[/bold] can be used to:
- select a net - rename a memory - clear a memory
Standard squad and command nets appear near the top of the net list.
Nets identified by the search receiver are marked [bold][INTERCEPT][/bold]. These nets can be monitored and logged, but the radio does not relay enemy nets.
[bold]Direct frequencies[/bold] are entered through the expert faceplate. They are unrelayed and unencrypted. Entering the frequency of a known net loads that net instead.
## Handset
Anyone can use the AN/PRC handset.
Alt-click the [bold]person wearing the radio[/bold], or a radio that has been staked down, and select [bold]Take Handset[/bold].
While holding the handset:
- normal speech is transmitted over the radio's ON AIR net - your own callsign is used - whispering does not transmit - only one person can use the handset at a time - moving roughly two and a half tiles from the radio causes the handset to return automatically
Use the handset with Z, or select [bold]Hang Up Handset[/bold], to return it.
The handset allows another person to transmit through the radio without needing direct access to its controls.
## Field telephone
The AN/PRC can place calls to:
- other AN/PRC radios - fixed command-post telephones - shipboard telephone stations
To place a call, use the [bold]AN/PRC-117G phone[/bold] action, select [bold]Use Phone[/bold] on the radio, or press [bold]PHONE[/bold] on the control panel.
Select an available station from the phone book.
When receiving a call:
- the radio wearer is shown the caller's station - taking the handset answers the call - the phone action can also answer the call - a person already holding the handset joins the call automatically
During a call, speech through the handset is sent to the telephone connection instead of the radio's ON AIR net.
Returning the handset ends the call.
The phone book identifies stations by [bold]callsign[/bold].
### Telephone requirements
A radio belongs to the faction associated with its installed [bold]COMSEC fill card[/bold].
A radio without a fill card cannot place or receive telephone calls.
For a telephone link to work, both stations must:
- be switched on - be worn or staked down - have sufficient power - not be inside heavy jamming - not be in EMCON
The stations must also either:
- be within roughly 45 tiles of each other - both have relay access through their faction's command net
Unreachable stations do not appear in the phone book.
If the radio link is lost during a call, the call ends.
Spoken telephone traffic consumes power and may produce a direction-finding signature.
## Storage
The AN/PRC contains a five-by-two storage compartment that accepts items up to Large size.
Click the radio pack to open it.
Fill cards, antennas, and power cells use their dedicated slots before entering the storage compartment.
[bold]Anyone standing beside a staked radio can access its storage compartment.[/bold]
## Battery
The AN/PRC runs from a power cell.
Active radio functions increase power consumption.
The radio operator's equipment rack provides three high-capacity cells. AN/PRC resupply crates contain two additional cells.
[bold]Radio activity[/bold] [bold]Approximate high-capacity cell endurance[/bold]
Powered on without relaying 80 minutes
Relaying squad traffic 55 minutes
Relaying and normal transmissions 40 to 45 minutes
Search receiver active Search adds 3 power per second
Additional power is consumed by:
- transmitting - radio checks - telephone traffic - retransmissions - frequency hopping - HI output power
The expert faceplate provides [bold]POWER SAVE[/bold] and [bold]EMCON[/bold] modes.
Its [bold]ENDURANCE[/bold] display estimates remaining operating time based on the radio's current power drain.
When the cell is depleted, the radio switches off. Replace the cell and switch the radio back on.
## Callsigns
Radio traffic identifies users by [bold]callsign[/bold].
Character names and job titles are not transmitted through headsets or the AN/PRC. Normal face-to-face speech is unaffected.
Callsigns are assigned automatically at deployment.
[bold]Example[/bold] [bold]Station[/bold]
HAVOC 6 Commanding officer
HAVOC 5 Executive officer or second-in-command
HAVOC 7 Senior non-commissioned officer
HAVOC ROMEO Command radio operator
HAVOC OPS Staff officers
SABRE ACTUAL Sabre squad leader
SABRE ROMEO Radio operator attached to Sabre
SABRE 1-1 ... 1-N Sabre squad members
[bold]ACTUAL[/bold] indicates that the person commanding the station is speaking personally.
A worn radio normally uses the [bold]wearer's callsign[/bold]. The faceplate displays this setting as AUTO.
The callsign automatically updates when:
- the wearer changes - the wearer changes squad - the radio is handed to another operator
Staked radios and command-post stations can instead be assigned a fixed [bold]station callsign[/bold] from the expert faceplate's OPT page.
The [bold]Comms Net Directory[/bold] shows which station currently holds each callsign. It is available from:
- [bold]NET DIRECTORY[/bold] on the radio panel - command-post laptops - overwatch consoles
For standard radio terminology, see [textlink="Voice Procedure" link="AU14CommsVoiceProcedure"].
## COMSEC and encryption
Radio encryption is stored on a physical [bold]COMSEC fill card[/bold].
With a current fill card installed, secured radio traffic is heard as static by hostile listeners without the matching key.
- [bold]No fill card[/bold] - the radio remains functional, but transmissions are sent in the clear. - [bold]PT[/bold] - deliberately transmits in the clear even when a valid fill card is installed. - [bold]ZEROIZE[/bold] - ejects the installed fill card. - [bold]DESTROY[/bold] - destroys the installed fill card. - [bold]RECRYPTO[/bold] - replaces the faction's current encryption key. Existing fill cards immediately become invalid. - A current [bold]captured enemy fill card[/bold] allows secured enemy traffic to be read until that faction performs a recrypto.
Replacement fill cards are normally obtained through supply.
Expert operators can also distribute a new key over the air through the faceplate's SEC page.
## Waveforms
The AN/PRC supports several transmission modes.
[bold]Mode[/bold] [bold]Effect[/bold] [bold]Limitations[/bold]
[bold]FH[/bold] frequency hop Reduces jamming by one tier. 1.5x transmission power cost and a small DF signature.
[bold]SC[/bold] single channel Low power cost. Secured SC produces no DF signature. No resistance to jamming.
[bold]CT[/bold] cipher text Unreadable without the matching fill card. Produces no DF signature. Requires a fill card. Ordinary headsets cannot receive CT.
[bold]PT[/bold] plain text Uses half the normal transmission power. Unencrypted and produces the largest DF signature.
Waveforms are selected from the expert faceplate.
The guided panel uses [bold]FH[/bold] automatically.
## Jamming and direction finding
Jamming degrades radio communications rather than automatically disabling them.
A manpack can continue transmitting inside a jammer field, but messages may be received in a degraded state.
[bold]FH[/bold] reduces jamming by one tier.
Heavy jamming prevents field-telephone connections.
Hostile electronic-warfare equipment may detect the location of radio transmissions.
Direction-finding risk increases with:
- PT transmissions - faction-net traffic transmitted without a fill card - FH transmissions - HI output power - repeated transmissions from the same position - transmissions made near a jammer
Secured SC and CT transmissions produce no DF signature.
The expert faceplate provides additional emission controls:
- [bold]BURST[/bold] halves detection chance - [bold]EMCON[/bold] prevents radio transmissions from producing a DF signature
### Radio check
[bold]RADIO CHECK[/bold] transmits [bold]RADIO CHECK, HOW COPY, OVER[/bold] on the current working net.
After the transmission, the radio reports:
- which stations received the message - whether reception was clear or degraded
If the radio is inside a jammer field, the check also provides an approximate bearing toward the jammer.
## Monitor and scan
The AN/PRC can listen to multiple loaded nets.
[bold]MONITOR[/bold]:
- listens to every loaded net - makes the radio receive-only - disables [color=#a4885c]:r[/color] transmissions while active
[bold]SCAN[/bold]:
- listens to every loaded net - changes ON AIR to whichever memory most recently received traffic - leaves that memory selected until another loaded net receives traffic or the operator changes it manually
Both modes are available from the guided SETTINGS tab and the expert faceplate's OPT page.
## Net log
The AN/PRC stores the last [bold]50[/bold] radio lines it processed.
The log can include:
- the operator's transmissions - traffic heard through the operator's headset - incoming traffic on the working net - traffic from all loaded nets while using MONITOR or SCAN
Enemy traffic is marked [bold]INTERCEPT[/bold].
[bold]PRINT LOG[/bold] prints the complete record.
[bold]PRINT INTERCEPTS[/bold] prints only intercepted traffic.
## Search and interception
Operational radio frequencies are reassigned each deployment.
Enemy nets can be discovered by:
- obtaining an enemy frequency card - using the AN/PRC search receiver
Search controls are located on the expert faceplate's SRCH page. See the [textlink="Expert faceplate" link="AU14CommsANPRCExpert"] guide for operating instructions.
[bold]While the search receiver is active, the radio leaves its loaded nets and cannot transmit.[/bold]
Intercepted traffic appears in radio chat as [color=#E09A3E][bold]INT[/bold][/color] messages.
Intercepts show:
- the intercepted net - the sender's callsign
They are also stored in the radio's net log.
Messages generated by the radio itself appear as [color=#7FC48C][bold]117G[/bold][/color] messages. Amber 117G messages indicate an error or refused action.
### Reading intercepted traffic
Whether an intercepted transmission can be read depends on how it was transmitted.
- Headset traffic without the correct key is heard as static. - Secured manpack traffic without the correct key is heard as static. - Traffic from a radio without a fill card is readable. - PT traffic is readable. - CT traffic is not displayed.
Once an enemy net has been identified, transmissions on that net can still provide direction-finding information even when their contents cannot be read.
Each detected transmission within range provides:
- a bearing toward the transmitter - a temporary tactical-map marker
Expert operators can also attempt to break an enemy net's key from the faceplate.
## Retransmission
A trained operator can convert the manpack into an unattended relay using [bold]Set Up Retrans[/bold].
A staked radio continues to:
- relay its loaded nets - retain its memories - retain its fill card - retain its radio log
Anyone standing beside a staked radio can:
- take its handset - use its telephone - access its storage compartment
The expert faceplate can also configure a staked radio to bridge two loaded nets.
[bold]Anyone can select Pack Up Radio on a staked radio.[/bold]
Packing up the radio removes the radio, handset, and installed fill card from the retransmission position.
## Fixed relays
Manpacks are not the only source of combat-net relay coverage.
- Powered shipboard [bold]communications arrays[/bold] provide coverage throughout their ship and across its decks. - Command-post [bold]antenna masts[/bold] provide 75 tiles of coverage without requiring power. - Engineers and RTOs can construct [bold]field antenna masts[/bold] to provide additional relay coverage.
A field mast only carries the nets of factions whose COMSEC keys have been loaded into it.
A field mast requires power to relay traffic.
## Field antenna mast
Engineering level 2 or RTO/JTAC level 4 training is required to construct and service a field antenna mast.
[bold]Antenna mast parts[/bold] are available from the metal-sheet construction menu.
### Construction
- Place the [bold]mast footing[/bold] using 40 metal. - The footing must be on open ground beneath open sky and outside underground areas. - There must be enough open space for the mast's guy lines. - The footing must be at least 20 tiles from another mast or communications array. - Invalid placement removes the footing and returns the metal. - Wrench the footing into place. - Add 30 metal rods. - Weld the lattice. - Add 15 cable for the guy lines. - Install a [bold]mast antenna head[/bold].
Mast antenna heads are available from requisitions.
An antenna head can also be constructed from an [bold]antenna head frame[/bold]:
- add 20 metal - add 40 plasteel - add four circuit boards - add 30 cable - weld the assembly - use a multitool
After installing the antenna head:
- add 10 plasteel to plate the feed - tune the feed with a multitool - use a [bold]COMSEC fill card[/bold] on the open feed to load that faction's key - repeat with additional faction fill cards if required - screw the feed closed - weld the feed
The mast is then operational.
Using a multitool on an open feed removes all stored COMSEC keys.
### Rekeying
To change the keys stored in an existing mast:
- open the feed with a screwdriver and wirecutters - insert the required COMSEC fill card - close and seal the feed again
The mast carries no radio traffic while its feed is open.
An open mast can be dismantled to recover most construction materials and the antenna head.
## CLF communications
The CLF use two relay-gated combat nets:
- [bold]CLF[/bold] - the cell's standard net, available on CLF earpieces - [bold]CLF Command[/bold] - available through AN/PRC radios
The CLF do not have a permanent communications array.
Their relay coverage is provided by deployable equipment, including:
- radio-operator manpacks - the cell's [bold]clandestine base station[/bold] - additional deployed relay radios
The issued CLF manpack begins tuned to both CLF combat nets.
The clandestine base station:
- cannot be worn - operates only while staked down - can use a mast antenna to cover the safehouse and surrounding area
Both the Cell Leader and Radio Operator receive communications equipment capable of deploying relay coverage.
If the CLF lose access to both combat nets, the [bold]Colony[/bold] channel remains available.
Colony is not relay-gated and is unencrypted.
